title: FHIR Validation Doesn't Tell You What to Do Next, So I Built a Decision Layer
summary:
A FHIR resource can pass validation and still be the wrong thing to act on. I built a small decision layer for that gap: it takes parsed FHIR R4 resources, sends a flattened state to TypeSafe AI's Jev model, and turns the answer into accept, route, flag or human review.

On 204 synthetic records, the first live run lost routing to my hand-written rules, 0.814 to 0.922, and missed too many notifiable diseases. Both failures came from my own setup. One was a serializer bug and the other was a badly framed routing question. After fixing both, Jev scored above the rules on all three decisions, on the same records. It still misses my latency target by a wide margin.

This is a proof of concept. It runs on synthetic data and it is not connected to any production system.

What validation does not answer

Here is part of a Patient that parses as FHIR R4:

{
  "resourceType": "Patient",
  "id": "invalid-nik",
  "identifier": [{"system": "nik", "value": "317301010190000"}],
  "name": [{"family": "Wijaya"}]
}

The NIK is Indonesia's national ID, and it has 16 digits. This one has 15. A Condition can have the same problem in a different form: well-formed, coded as dengue, with verificationStatus set to refuted. The patient does not have dengue, and the resource is still structurally correct.

Conformance checking answers one question: does this resource meet the spec? A pipeline has to answer a different one: what should happen to this resource now?

Conformance Decision layer
Question Does it meet the spec? What do we do with it?
Output Pass or fail, with issues An action and a confidence
Defined by Spec and profiles Workflow and risk tolerance
When unsure Does not apply Sends it to a person

Profiles can cover more of this than people expect. A FHIRPath invariant could enforce a 16-digit NIK, so that example does not need a model. The boundary I care about is not rules versus AI. It is is this correct? versus what happens next?

The pipeline

Jev is a decision model. It takes a structured state and a fixed question, and returns a typed answer with a confidence. It does not generate text. The project uses its three primitives: Choice picks one option from a list, Score returns a number on a scale, and Noul answers a statement with a probability that it is true.

The service is FastAPI with Pydantic v2, and it makes three decisions:

Decision Primitive Output
Is this resource good enough to accept automatically? Score, plus Noul for the NIK Score 0 to 100, then accept or review
Which pipeline should get this Bundle? Choice One of five fixed categories
Must this Condition be reported? Noul Probability, plus a Flag when confirmed

Conformance runs first, then the state gets small

Every serializer parses the resource before it extracts anything. A resource that fails parsing raises an error, so no Jev call happens. This is lighter than full profile and terminology validation, but the order is the design: conformance first, decisions on top.

# src/jev_fhir/serializer/patient.py
def serialize(self, resource: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Validate a Patient and produce a missing-field-safe flat state."""
    Patient.parse_obj(resource)

    identifier = first_mapping(resource.get("identifier"))
    identifier_value = identifier.get("value") if identifier is not None else None

    return {
        "resource_type": self.resource_type(),
        "has_identifier": identifier is not None,
        "identifier_value_length": len(identifier_value)
        if isinstance(identifier_value, str)
        else None,
        # remaining demographic fields omitted
    }

The model never receives the NIK itself, only its length. This is the state produced from the full version of that Patient:

{
  "resource_type": "Patient",
  "has_identifier": true,
  "identifier_system": "nik",
  "identifier_value_length": 15,
  "has_name": true,
  "name_family": "Wijaya",
  "has_birth_date": true,
  "has_gender": true,
  "has_address": true,
  "address_country": "ID",
  "has_telecom": false,
  "telecom_count": 0,
  "field_completeness": 8,
  "field_total": 10
}

A small state keeps each call cheap and easy to inspect. The demo UI shows this exact state next to every decision, which made debugging much easier later. It is not a privacy solution, though. name_family is still in there, and real data would need a proper review.

A probability is not an action

Thresholds turn a model output into something the pipeline can do. The router has a confidence floor, and anything below it becomes unknown:

# src/jev_fhir/modules/bundle_router.py
state = self._serializer.serialize(bundle)
result = await self._jev_client.choice(state, ROUTE_QUESTION, ROUTE_OPTIONS)
category = result.choice if result.confidence >= confidence_minimum else "unknown"

The quality scorer treats the NIK as a gate. A high completeness score cannot override it:

# src/jev_fhir/modules/quality_scorer.py
passes_nik_gate = nik_valid is not False
action = (
    "auto_accept"
    if score_result.score >= threshold and passes_nik_gate
    else "review_needed"
)

Notifiable detection uses two thresholds, which gives it a band for human review:


# src/jev_fhir/modules/notifiable_detector.py
if result.probability >= confirmed_threshold and result.answer:
    status = "confirmed_notifiable"
    is_notifiable = True
    # builds the FHIR Flag here
elif result.probability >= review_threshold:
    status = "review_needed"
    is_notifiable = False
    flag_resource = None
else:
    status = "not_notifiable"
    is_notifiable = False
    flag_resource = None

The review band is the part conformance has no equivalent for. The system can say it is not sure, and that outcome has a defined place to go.

How I measured it

I compared Jev with a transparent rule baseline for each decision. The rules are deliberately simple: a field-count score, a length check for the NIK, routing on resource types and LOINC signals, and an exact ICD-10 lookup.

The dataset has 204 labelled fixtures, including a hard set built to separate semantic judgment from exact matching. Labels are never computed from the logic under test. The test suite uses a mock Jev client and never calls the live API, and the benchmark runs against the live model only when I ask it to.

Decision Fixtures Jev, first run Jev, final Rules My target
Quality (accuracy) 71 0.676 0.662 0.549 ≥ 0.85, missed
Routing (accuracy) 102 0.814 0.951 0.922 ≥ 0.90, met
Notifiable (accuracy) 31 0.839 0.935 0.677 none set
Notifiable (recall) 31 0.737 0.895 0.579 ≥ 0.95, missed
Notifiable (precision) 31 1.000 1.000 0.846 ≥ 0.80, met

The rest of this article explains how the first-run column became the final one.

The bug the state panel exposed

My first live run scored 0.839 on notifiable detection, with a recall of 0.737. The score alone gave no hint of why.

The cause showed up while I was reviewing the demo. The state panel for a text-only dengue case showed code_value, code_display and code_system all null, with no disease name anywhere. My serializer read code.coding and never read code.text, so the model was judging a blank. Three of the five misses had the disease name only in code.text, such as "Demam berdarah dengue (DBD)" and "TB paru".

The fix is small:

# src/jev_fhir/serializer/condition.py
+CODE_TEXT_MAX_LENGTH = 200

         code = resource.get("code")
+        code_text = code.get("text") if isinstance(code, dict) else None
         onset = resource.get("onsetDateTime")

             "code_display": first_coding_value(code, "display"),
+            "code_text": code_text[:CODE_TEXT_MAX_LENGTH] if isinstance(code_text, str) else None,
             "clinical_status": first_coding_code(resource.get("clinicalStatus")),

The 200-character limit keeps a long note from inflating token use and limits how much free text leaves the system. I kept the rule baseline code-only, so the comparison stayed fair. I also kept the mock code-only, because teaching it to read text would make mock results look like model evidence.

I then compared the two live reports row by row. Exactly three notifiable rows changed, and they were the three I expected:

Fixture Confidence before Confidence after Result
dbd_text_only 0.47 0.90 wrong → correct
tb_paru_text_only 0.50 0.89 wrong → correct
condition_dbd_text_only 0.49 0.89 wrong → correct

Accuracy went from 0.839 to 0.935, and recall went from 0.737 to 0.895. The earlier score was measuring my pipeline, not the model. Without the row-level comparison, I could not have told that apart from noise, because quality accuracy moved from 0.676 to 0.648 between the same two runs on rows the fix does not touch.

The two remaining misses, B20 HIV and typhoid A01.0, have proper codes. Both landed in the review band at about 0.77, so a person would see them. All 19 notifiable cases were either confirmed or sent to review, and none was dismissed.

Why rules first won routing

My first explanation for the routing loss was that routing is mostly clear logic. I had written that down, but I had not measured it. So I compared the flat state of every Bundle Jev got right and wrong.

All 12 of its encounter errors followed one pattern:

Conditions in the Bundle Bundles Jev correct
1 6 6
2 2 1
3 or more 11 0

Both live runs showed this, and 100 of the 102 routing decisions were identical across the runs. This was a systematic failure, not noise.

Two things in my setup could explain it. The question was "What type of clinical data does this FHIR Bundle primarily contain?". One Encounter with eight Conditions primarily contains Conditions, and no category exists for that, so unknown was a fair answer. The same word would also explain the other errors, because all seven misrouted mixed Bundles went to the pipeline for their most common resource type.

The state was also uneven. It had direct flags for labs, immunizations and medications, which scored at 1.00 confidence, but nothing direct for encounters. dominant_resource_type said Condition.

I changed both:

# src/jev_fhir/modules/bundle_router.py
-ROUTE_QUESTION = "What type of clinical data does this FHIR Bundle primarily contain?"
+ROUTE_QUESTION = "Which processing pipeline should handle this FHIR Bundle?"

# src/jev_fhir/serializer/bundle.py
             "contains_medication": "MedicationDispense" in resource_types,
+            "contains_encounter": "Encounter" in resource_types,

To see which change mattered, I ran the flag on its own first:

Live routing run Accuracy 3+ Condition Bundles correct
Original 0.814 0 of 11
Flag only 0.863 4 of 11
Flag and new question 0.951 11 of 11

Fourteen rows improved and none got worse. The question did most of the work, which I did not expect. It was one sentence, and it had been costing more than the missing data.

The rule baseline stayed the same, and a test confirms it does not use the new field. In the final run Jev was right on three Bundles the rules got wrong, and the reverse never happened. That margin is small, so I would not read it as a clear win. The rules scored 0.922 with no model at all.

Five mixed Bundles are still wrong, and three of those are at 0.87 confidence or higher, so the floor does not catch them. One of them, vitals_only, has a label I have not settled. The rules' 0.95 on generated Bundles also needs care: the rule checks has_encounter_reference, and my generator links every generated encounter Bundle that way, so the two share a signal.

Where each side won

Jev did best where the decision depends on more than one field. On the 14 hard Condition fixtures it scored 0.929 against 0.357 for the rules. The rules reported a refuted dengue case and a cholera record marked entered-in-error as real. Jev confirmed neither, and both went to review. It also caught dengue and tuberculosis coded only in SNOMED, which an ICD-10 lookup cannot see.

Some of that gap is cheap to close. Prefix matching would handle subcodes like A15.0, and checking verificationStatus would handle the refuted case. A serious rule set would do both.

For routing, the rules remain the sensible default. They are simple and free, and a model can act as a second opinion, with disagreements going to a person.

Quality scoring is the weakest result. Of 45 records that needed review, Jev let 14 through and the rules let 32 through. But Jev also held 10 of 26 good records, and the rules held none.

Confidence only works where it is calibrated

A threshold is only useful if confidence means something, so the benchmark buckets decisions by confidence and compares that with observed accuracy. This is the top bucket:

Decision Count Mean confidence Observed accuracy
Notifiable 17 0.844 1.000
Routing 84 0.982 0.964
Quality 24 0.825 0.667

Notifiable looks trustworthy here, and routing improved after the question change, from 0.918 in this bucket. Quality does not: a confidence of 0.82 was right about two times in three, so I would not automate anything on that threshold yet.

What it gets wrong

Latency. My target was a p50 under 30 ms. The live p50 was about 235 ms for routing and notifiable, and 458 ms for quality, where a Patient takes two calls. The p95 ranged from 263 ms to 510 ms. These are client-side round trips from my machine, so they include the network, and I have not separated model time. The fast-decision premise is not proven by this data.

Cost target. The full run used 147,401 tokens for about $0.006. That is about $0.03 per 1,000 records, three times my $0.01 target. It is still very cheap.

Evaluation quality. No human has approved the labels yet. 124 are pending review, and the other 80 are correct by construction because a generator produced them. The hard sets are small. I also made both fixes after seeing these same fixtures fail, so 0.935 and 0.951 are not held-out results. They need confirming on data the system has not seen.

What comes next

The first step is human review of the labels, because every number here depends on them. After that I want a held-out set for the notifiable and routing decisions, and a latency measurement that separates the network from the model. Two gaps from this work are still open: ObservationSerializer drops code.text the same way the Condition serializer did, and all the serializers read only the first coding.

The result I would keep is the shape of the system, more than any single score: parse first, flatten to a state a person can inspect, use a threshold per decision, give uncertain cases a lane, and keep a baseline that can beat the model. That baseline did beat it, and that is why I went looking. Before blaming a model, I now check what it actually received and what I actually asked.

title: Memoir de Ofrenda: A Local-First Día de los Muertos Memory Altar (Ghost in the Machine)
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Between late October and early November—as Halloween shifts into Día de los Muertos—the boundary between past and present feels remarkably thin. We set out ofrendas, light candles, and gather the favorite foods, songs, and stories of people whose voices once filled our kitchens.

title: Build a Self-Supervised Pretext Task in 25 Lines of Python (No Labels Required)
summary:
Most teams don't have a data problem. They have a label problem: millions of raw documents or images and only a few thousand annotated ones. Self-supervised learning (SSL) gets around this by making the data label itself.

The easiest way to understand that is to build the label generator yourself. Here's a minimal masked-token pretext task, the same idea BERT is pretrained with, in plain Python.

Step 1: Start with raw, unlabeled text 

corpus = [
    "the engineer deployed the model to production",
    "the server returned an unexpected error",
    "the model detected a damaged component",
]

No sentiment tags, no categories, no annotators.

Step 2: Turn every sentence into (input, target) pairs automatically 

import random

MASK = "[MASK]"

def make_pretext_examples(sentence, mask_prob=0.15, seed=None):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    tokens = sentence.split()
    inputs, targets = [], []
    for tok in tokens:
        if rng.random() < mask_prob:
            inputs.append(MASK)
            targets.append(tok)      # the hidden word is the label
        else:
            inputs.append(tok)
            targets.append(None)     # no loss on visible tokens
    return inputs, targets

for i, s in enumerate(corpus):
    print(make_pretext_examples(s, mask_prob=0.3, seed=i))

Output (Python 3, exactly as printed):

(['the', 'engineer', 'deployed', '[MASK]', 'model', 'to', 'production'], [None, None, None, 'the', None, None, None])
(['[MASK]', 'server', 'returned', '[MASK]', 'unexpected', 'error'], ['the', None, None, 'an', None, None])
(['the', 'model', '[MASK]', '[MASK]', 'damaged', 'component'], [None, None, 'detected', 'a', None, None])

Notice the first two sentences mostly hid easy words like "the" and "an". That's exactly the shortcut problem covered below; real pipelines mask subword tokens and use smarter masking strategies.

That's the whole trick. The target came from the original sentence. Nobody wrote it by hand.

Step 3: What a real model does with these pairs

In a real pipeline you would:

  1. Tokenize with a subword tokenizer instead of split()
  2. Feed inputs to a Transformer encoder
  3. Compute cross-entropy only on the masked positions (the Nones are ignored)
  4. Repeat over millions of sentences

The encoder can't predict "detected" in the third example without understanding that models detect damaged components, so it ends up learning syntax and meaning as a side effect. That side effect, a reusable representation, is what you actually want.

Step 4: Throw away the head, keep the encoder

After pretraining, you discard the token-prediction head and fine-tune the encoder on your small labeled dataset (say, 2,000 support tickets tagged by intent). This is where SSL pays off: far fewer labels for the same accuracy.

Three gotchas we learned the hard way

  • Too-easy masks teach shortcuts. Masking only stop-words ("the", "a") gives the model nothing to learn.
  • Masking is a design decision. In images, a random crop can cut out the exact defect or tumour you care about. Choose transformations that keep the meaning you need downstream.
  • Low pretraining loss ≠ a useful model. Evaluate with a linear probe and with fine-tuning on the real task.

Beyond masking

Masked modeling is one of four big SSL objective families. The others are contrastive learning (SimCLR), teacher-student methods without negatives (BYOL), and redundancy reduction (Barlow Twins, VICReg). We cover all four, plus a decision framework and how to evaluate SSL models properly, in our complete guide: Self-Supervised Learning Explained: How AI Learns Without Labeled Data.

What would you mask in your own dataset? Tell us in the comments.

— The AheadMint Team

title: How long a liquor license takes in Texas, New York City and Los Angeles (data from 1,000+ applications)
summary:
Disclosure: I run PourWire, which turns state liquor license and building permit filings into a daily list of restaurants and bars that are about to open. The numbers below come from that pipeline plus the states' own open data. The CSV is public under CC BY 4.0.

The question "how long does a liquor license take" has a different answer in every state, and most answers online are guesses. Here is what the filings say as of October 2026.

The short answer

Where Agency Typical time Measured on
Texas (5 metros) TABC median 24 days from submission to issue (middle half 18 to 34) 144 MB and BG applications filed since June 2026
New York City NY State Liquor Authority applications pending a median of 118 days (middle half 62 to 212); 32% over 6 months 920 restaurant and bar applications pending in the five boroughs
Los Angeles County California ABC median 67 days from application to issue (middle half 54 to 72) 23 issued type 41, 47 and 48 licenses filed since July 2026

How it was measured

Texas. TABC publishes pending applications and issued licenses as two datasets on data.texas.gov. We matched our MB (mixed beverage) and BG (wine and beer) applications in Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin, San Antonio and Waco-Temple to the original issue date in TABC License Information by owner and permit.

New York City. The SLA queue is the story. data.ny.gov "Current SLA Pending Licenses" lists every application still in review with its received date, so the age of what is waiting today is the honest number. Of the NYC applications we have tracked since June, 25 have been issued so far, a median of 105 days after the SLA received them. That figure is capped by our start date, so the real average is higher.

Los Angeles. California ABC keeps one license number from application to issue, so filing to issue is a direct join. Every new application goes through a 30-day public notice period before ABC investigates, which is why almost nothing issues in under a month (the fastest we saw was 36 days).

Get the data

  • CSV of the wait times with sample sizes and source links: us-liquor-license-applications on GitHub (data/liquor-license-wait-times.csv), plus the last 30 days of new applications across every metro we track, refreshed weekly. Also on Hugging Face.
  • Step by step lookup guides with the license class codes explained:
    • Texas: pending TABC applications, MB, BG and FB
    • New York City: SLA wait times, classes 340, 240 and 370
    • Los Angeles: ABC wait times, types 41, 47 and 48

If you are opening a restaurant, the practical takeaway is to file early in New York, budget about two months in Los Angeles, and expect about a month in Texas. If you sell to new restaurants, the pending lists are a 1 to 4 month head start on who is about to open.

Corrections and better joins are welcome in the GitHub repo issues.

title: What if the history of a codebase could help explain the code nobody wants to touch?
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

NecroGit: A Little Séance for Legacy Code

Every codebase has a past.

Sometimes that past is a beautifully maintained changelog. Sometimes it is a function named do_not_delete_final2(), three deprecated imports, and a Git history that only the person who wrote it really understood.

Then that person leaves.

The code stays.

For Week 4's Ghost in the Machine challenge, I built NecroGit: a command-line tool that treats legacy-code maintenance like a bit of software archaeology. It looks for signs of bitrot, examines Git history for clues about how a project evolved, and uses an open-weight language model to help explain unfamiliar code and propose repairs.

The goal isn't to pretend a model can bring a developer back from the dead. It's to make the traces they left behind more useful to the next person who has to maintain the project.

What I Built

NecroGit is a Python CLI for developers inheriting repositories they didn't write.

It brings a few kinds of investigation into one workflow:

  • Inspect: scan Python files for known deprecated APIs and suspicious legacy patterns.
  • Summon: examine Git commits and author activity for historical context.
  • Explain: ask a language model to explain an unfamiliar function using the source and available repository context.
  • Patch: generate a proposed diff that a developer can review before applying.
  • Memory: keep a small repository dossier so useful context can carry between sessions.

The part I care about most is the connection between these steps. Finding a deprecated import is useful. Understanding why the surrounding code exists is better. Getting a proposed change that you can inspect, test, and reject if necessary is better still.

NecroGit is meant to assist the maintainer, not replace their judgment. Git history can offer clues about a previous developer's habits; it cannot tell us with certainty what that person intended. Likewise, an AI-generated patch is a proposal, not proof that the fix is correct.

Demo

Repository: github.com/avrojitduttaj/necrogit

The quickest way to see the workflow is to install the project in a Python environment, open a repository in your terminal, and try the inspection command:

necrogit inspect .

Then explore the other commands with:

necrogit --help
necrogit summon .
necrogit memory

The exact arguments for explain and patch depend on the installed CLI version; check each command's --help before running it.

Live demo / walkthrough: [Add a verified demo URL or video here]

I don't want to pass off a mockup as a working demo, so this post links to the source repository. If I add a hosted walkthrough, I'll put the verified URL here.

Code

The source is available here:

Explore NecroGit on GitHub

Live Deployment: NecroGit — The Repository Medium

A few of the implementation choices:

  • Python's ast module provides a structured way to inspect source code without executing it.
  • GitPython reads repository history and commit metadata.
  • Click provides the command-line interface, with Rich for readable terminal output.
  • HTTPX connects the engine to an OpenAI-compatible local model endpoint.
  • Repository dossiers can be stored locally, with optional Backboard integration in the project.

The intent is to keep the first step—static inspection—useful even when an AI model isn't available. The AI-assisted commands should fail clearly when inference isn't configured, rather than pretending they succeeded.

How I Built It

I built NecroGit around a simple question: what if Git history were more than a list of commits?

The scanner handles the deterministic part. It parses Python syntax and checks for patterns the tool knows about. The Git-history component gathers evidence such as authorship, commit dates, and commit messages. The AI engine can then use the available code and context to generate an explanation or a proposed diff.

For the open-model path, NecroGit is designed to work with Gemma 2 through Ollama, using a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. That makes it possible to experiment with the model on your own machine rather than making a hosted, closed API the only way to run the project.

This separation matters:

  1. Rules find known patterns. They are predictable, testable, and don't need a model.
  2. Git history supplies evidence. It gives context, but it isn't a source of certainty about intent.
  3. The model helps interpret and draft. It can explain code and suggest changes, but its output still needs review and tests.

During development, I also added tests for deprecated-import detection, Git and non-Git directories, prompt construction, connection failures, local memory persistence, and CLI behavior. Those tests have been useful for catching mismatches between the intended user experience and what the command actually does.

One lesson from building a CLI is that a feature isn't finished just because the Python function works. Packaging, command registration, Windows paths, model endpoints, and readable error messages are all part of the product. I'm still tightening those edges, and I want to be honest about that rather than call the tool production-ready before it earns the label.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a tool that reads source code, where inference happens is part of the design.

A developer may be working with a private repository, a client's code, or an abandoned internal service. Sending that code to an external API should never be an invisible default. A local model gives the developer a path to keep inference on their own machine, subject to how they've configured the rest of their environment.

Open-weight models also make the system more replaceable. Developers can experiment with different models and local runtimes instead of tying the whole experience to one provider's API, pricing, or product decisions.

And the non-AI parts remain ordinary, inspectable software. The scanner's rules can be read and tested. The Git-history analysis can be audited. A proposed patch is visible as a diff.

That doesn't mean every setup is automatically offline or private: optional integrations and telemetry need to be configured and disclosed carefully. But open tooling gives developers more control over those trade-offs—and for a maintenance tool that may touch sensitive code, that control is important.

My Agent Session

[https://dev.to/agent_sessions/finding-the-necrogit-devrelay-session-link-xmpym5]

This section is optional. I will only link a real saved session; I won't invent an embed or session URL.

The Spirit of It

There's something eerie about opening a repository and finding a whole history of decisions with nobody left to explain them.

A commit message says “temporary workaround.” The workaround is still there six years later. A function has a strange name because it once fixed a production incident. A dependency is obsolete, but nobody remembers which behavior relied on it.

The ghost isn't really the old developer. It's the missing context.

NecroGit is my attempt to make that context a little easier to recover—from the code, from the commit history, and from the tools we can run ourselves. Not to resurrect the past exactly as it was, but to help the next maintainer move forward without blindly deleting it.

🏆 Prize Categories I'm Targeting

  • [ ] Overall Challenge Winner — $250

    NecroGit aims to make legacy-code maintenance easier by combining Git-history archaeology, AI-assisted code explanations, and safer patch proposals.

  • [ ] Best Use of Gemma — $200

    Gemma 2 powers NecroGit's local AI inference workflow, helping explain historical design decisions and draft modernization patches while keeping source code on the developer's machine.

  • [ ] Best Use of Backboard — $100

    NecroGit implements persistent repository dossiers, with local JSON storage and an optional Backboard synchronization path for retaining maintainer context across sessions.

  • [ ] Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing — $100

    NecroGit includes instrumentation for tracing AI inference and memory operations, with breadcrumbs and structured context to help diagnose the resurrection workflow.

Deployment

NecroGit's web workbench is deployed on Render to make the project website accessible online. Render is used as a hosting and deployment platform, not as an AI integration.

The core NecroGit CLI remains a local developer tool, while the hosted website serves as the public-facing project experience.

Built by @avrojitduttaj.

If you've inherited a codebase that feels haunted, I'd love to know: what's the strangest piece of legacy code you've had to explain?

title: How to Export Google Ads Transparency Center Data (with Ad Copy) in Python
summary:
I wanted something simple: every Google search ad a competitor is running, how long each one has been running, and the actual ad copy — in a spreadsheet.

Google already publishes all of this in the Ads Transparency Center (Google's answer to Meta's Ad Library). It just has no export button and no API. So I scraped it, and ran into something I didn't expect: for most big advertisers, the ad copy isn't there as text at all.

The surprise: most text ads are stored as images

When you open a text ad in the Transparency Center, Google renders it in one of two ways:

  1. A text preview — the headline and description exist as text (in a small JS preview), easy to parse.
  2. A screenshot — a PNG of the ad, nothing else. The words only exist as pixels.

I pulled the first 30 text ads of five large advertisers on Nov 1, 2026 and counted how many had a text version:

Advertiser Text ads checked With a text version
booking.com 30 0
expedia.com 30 0
hubspot.com 30 1
samsung.com 30 7
nike.com 30 21
Total 150 29 (19%)

So if a tool only reads the text preview, the best it can do here is copy for about 1 ad in 5 — and for booking.com and expedia.com, nothing. That's a big hole if "what are my competitors saying?" is the whole point.

Reading the screenshots (the DIY version)

The fix is OCR. Each ad record links to its snapshot image (tpc.googlesyndication.com/archive/simgad/...), and a basic version with Tesseract is a few lines:

import io, requests, pytesseract
from PIL import Image

def read_ad(image_url):
    img = Image.open(io.BytesIO(requests.get(image_url, timeout=20).content)).convert("L")
    img = img.resize((img.width * 2, img.height * 2))          # small text OCRs better when upscaled
    data = pytesseract.image_to_data(img, config="--psm 6", output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT)
    words = [(w, float(c)) for w, c in zip(data["text"], data["conf"]) if w.strip() and float(c) >= 0]
    text = " ".join(w for w, _ in words)
    confidence = sum(c for _, c in words) / max(len(words), 1)
    return text, confidence

That gets you a blob of text. Turning it into headline / description / display URL reliably took most of the work. The traps I hit:

  1. Not everything in the image is the ad. Many snapshots include a product thumbnail or sitelink buttons on the right. OCR happily reads those and mixes them into the description. Detect and crop them first.
  2. Headline vs. description. Google draws the headline in blue and the description in dark grey, so splitting by color before OCR works far better than guessing from line positions afterwards.
  3. Language. The same advertiser runs ads in dozens of languages. Picking the Tesseract model from the countries the ad ran in (Korean, Japanese, Thai, Arabic, Cyrillic…) fixes most of the garbage.
  4. Trust the confidence score — strictly. My first threshold was 70. At 77, one booking.com description came out as "Book a Hotel near Universal Studios. HEHHE HAHA Quick, Easy Booking." Above 90 the text was mostly clean, apart from cut-off words. Anything lower should be flagged, not trusted.
  5. Some words are simply cut off. The screenshot crops long headlines, so you'll get "Hotels in Downtown Chica…". Nothing to fix there — just know it.
  6. Be gentle with Google. The listing endpoints rate-limit quickly (429s and CAPTCHA pages). Retry a couple of times, then stop — don't hammer.

The no-maintenance version

I packaged all of this as an Apify Actor (Google Ads Transparency & Ad Library Scraper), so I don't have to babysit OCR models or rate limits. Here's how I find a competitor's long-running search ads — the ones they keep paying for:

from apify_client import ApifyClient
import pandas as pd

client = ApifyClient("")

run = client.actor("datalume/google-ads-transparency-scraper").call(run_input={
    "domains": ["nike.com"],
    "region": "US",
    "platform": "search",
    "format": "text",
    "minDaysRunning": 30,          # skip short tests
    "sortBy": "longestRunning",
    "maxAdsPerTarget": 50,
})

df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())
good = df[df["copyStatus"] == "ok"]   # high-confidence copy only
good[["daysShown", "firstShown", "headline", "regionCount"]].head(10)

Here's what came back for nike.com (US, search, text ads, run on Nov 1, 2026) — 50 ads, copy for all 50 (38 from the text preview, 12 by OCR, all above 90 confidence). A slice of the longest-running ones:

Days shown First shown Advertiser Headline Countries
1,833 2021-10-25 WPP Media (agency) Zapatillas Air Max 90. Nike MX 8
1,794 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike - Onlineshop Deutschland 46
1,794 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike: zapatillas, ropa y más 51
1,793 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike UK - Online Store 44
1,792 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV The Official Nike Site - Nike: Shop The Collection (OCR) 39
1,735 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV NIKE — onlinebutik - Officiella Nike-webbplatsen (OCR) 29
1,384 2022-11-30 Nike, Inc. Training & Gym Equipment. Nike.com (OCR) 1
1,384 2022-11-30 Nike, Inc. (dynamic — Google writes it) 1

A few things jump out in under a minute:

  1. The longest-running ads weren't placed by Nike's own account but by an agency account (WPP Media). A domain search returns every advertiser whose ads point at the domain — useful, but filter by advertiser if you only want the brand itself.
  2. Nike's European "brand" ads have been running since at least October 2021, in roughly 30–50 countries each, with the same handful of lines ("The Official Website. Home Of Everything Nike. Shop The Latest Releases."). That's what a proven, evergreen brand ad looks like.
  3. In the US, 28 of the 31 ads from the Nike, Inc. account have no fixed headline — they're Dynamic Search Ads, where Google writes the headline from the landing page. Nike US leans on DSA and only controls the description. You'd never see that pattern by clicking through ads one at a time.

Also note daysShown is the number of days the ad actually ran, not just last-minus-first: three ads that all "started" on 2021-10-25 show 1,833, 1,794 and 1,688 days.

What else is in each row

  • firstShown, lastShown, daysShown, isActive — how long the ad has been running and whether it's live
  • regions — every country the ad ran in, with the last date shown there
  • headline, description, displayUrl, plus copySource (text or ocr) and copyConfidence
  • transparencyUrl — a link back to the ad on Google's site, so you can check anything by eye

You can also pass advertiser names or IDs instead of domains, filter by country / platform / date, and set onlyNewAds on a daily schedule to get just the new creatives.

Caveats (read these before you trust the numbers)

  • firstShown has a floor. The oldest ads I've seen all show 2021-10-25, which looks like where the Transparency Center's history begins. Read it as "running since at least then", not as the real start date.
  • OCR isn't perfect. Even high-confidence rows can contain a wrong letter ("Al" for "AI") or a cut-off word. Low-confidence rows are kept but marked lowConfidence.
  • Domain searches include other advertisers — agencies, resellers, or anyone whose ads link to that domain or its subdomains (like the WPP Media rows above). Use an advertiser ID if you need exactly one advertiser.

Cost

The Actor charges per ad: $2.00 per 1,000 ads, or $3.50 per 1,000 for text ads where high-confidence copy was extracted (instead of, not on top of, the $2). Countries are included, and rows Google fails to load are free. The 50-ad run above cost $0.18 (50 ads with copy × $0.0035) and took about a minute; with onlyNewAds on a schedule, you only pay for ads you haven't seen before.

title: Un pipeline de clima del Perú con dbt, DuckDB y GitHub Actions, sin AWS
summary:
Introducción

Un proyecto de ingeniería de datos puede empezar con una necesidad concreta y pocas herramientas: obtener datos públicos, transformarlos de forma reproducible y facilitar su consulta. Para este proyecto individual elegí comparar el clima de Lima, Arequipa y Cusco mediante una ventana de 30 días.

El código está en el repositorio público data-engineering-pipeline y el reporte puede consultarse en GitHub Pages. Ambos enlaces fueron comprobados después del primer despliegue.

Video de presentación

En este video muestro la funcionalidad de la solución: la consulta del reporte, la comparación entre ciudades, la descarga de datos y la actualización automatizada.

Ver la demostración funcional en YouTube.

El problema

Las respuestas de una API son útiles, pero no bastan para analizar datos de forma repetible. Pueden faltar fechas, aparecer nulos o acumularse duplicados si cargamos varias veces el mismo período. Además, una comparación entre ciudades necesita unidades, fechas y reglas de cálculo consistentes.

Mi objetivo fue construir un flujo pequeño que convierta respuestas meteorológicas en dos productos: una tabla diaria limpia y un resumen por ciudad. El resultado se exporta a un reporte HTML y archivos CSV.

Arquitectura y herramientas 

Open-Meteo → Python → JSON crudo + DuckDB raw.weather
                              ↓
                       dbt stg_weather
                              ↓
                       dbt city_summary
                              ↓
                    pruebas de calidad
                              ↓
                   HTML + CSV + metadatos
                              ↓
                   GitHub Pages, tras CD
  • Python 3.12 extrae respuestas HTTP, valida los datos y exporta los resultados.
  • DuckDB almacena tablas analíticas en un archivo, sin administrar un servidor.
  • dbt Core y dbt-duckdb gestionan las transformaciones SQL, sus dependencias y las pruebas.
  • GitHub Actions ejecuta CI, la actualización diaria y el despliegue.
  • GitHub Pages es el destino configurado para alojar el reporte estático públicamente.

No se utilizan servicios ni credenciales de AWS. La arquitectura usa GitHub como plataforma SaaS y no necesita un proceso Python funcionando permanentemente. Para esta escala, dbt permite demostrar transformación y calidad sin desplegar un orquestador de larga duración.

Implementación

1. Extraer una ventana consistente

La fuente es la API histórica de Open-Meteo. Para cada ciudad se solicitan temperatura máxima, mínima y precipitación diaria. La ventana termina siete días antes de la fecha actual en Lima para dejar margen a la disponibilidad del histórico.

Antes de cargar, Python comprueba las 30 fechas esperadas, las longitudes de las listas, valores numéricos finitos, coherencia entre mínima y máxima y precipitación no negativa. Cada petición tiene un timeout y hasta tres intentos. Si falla, la ejecución termina con error: no reemplaza los datos reales por datos sintéticos.

2. Cargar sin duplicar

Después de validar las tres ciudades, una transacción reemplaza raw.weather en DuckDB. Es una reconstrucción completa de una ventana pequeña. Repetir una ejecución no debe multiplicar registros.

Se conservan también las respuestas JSON para inspeccionar la fuente. Este diseño no pretende guardar un histórico incremental ilimitado: prioriza que el proyecto pueda entenderse, ejecutarse y evaluarse con facilidad.

3. Transformar con dbt

stg_weather tipifica los campos. city_summary utiliza ref('stg_weather'), por lo que dbt conoce el orden de construcción:

select city, min(date) as start_date, max(date) as end_date,
       count(*) as days,
       round(avg((temperature_max + temperature_min) / 2), 2) as mean_midpoint_c,
       round(max(temperature_max), 2) as highest_c,
       round(min(temperature_min), 2) as lowest_c,
       round(sum(precipitation_mm), 2) as total_precipitation_mm
from {{ ref('stg_weather') }}
group by city

El indicador mean_midpoint_c es el promedio del punto medio entre mínima y máxima diaria. Lo etiqueté así porque no equivale a calcular una media de temperaturas horarias. La fuente contiene reanálisis; tampoco debe presentarse como medición de una estación local.

4. Probar y generar la salida

dbt build construye dos modelos y ejecuta nueve pruebas de datos: campos obligatorios, unicidad, duplicados, rangos y continuidad de la ventana. Solo después se exportan el reporte y los CSV.

Las pruebas unitarias de Python cubren respuestas válidas, mediciones inválidas, fechas incorrectas y fallos de red. El modo --offline usa una fixture sintética identificada como TEST y escribe en otra carpeta. CI lo ejecuta dos veces para comprobar idempotencia y agregados conocidos.

Para reproducirlo en Linux o macOS con Python 3.12:

python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python -m pipeline.run --offline --end-date 2026-01-30
python -m pipeline.run

El README incluye los comandos equivalentes para PowerShell. El reporte real queda en site/public/index.html.

Despliegue y automatización

El workflow versionado separa tres trabajos. test ejecuta pruebas y datos sintéticos. build depende de las pruebas y utiliza la API real. deploy publica exclusivamente site/public en Pages y comprueba el endpoint público por HTTP.

Las PR solo ejecutan pruebas. Un push a main, una ejecución manual o la programación diaria producen una nueva actualización real. La programación está configurada a las 06:17 de Lima; GitHub puede retrasar ejecuciones programadas.

Para activar la publicación hay que seleccionar Settings → Pages → Source → GitHub Actions en el repositorio y ejecutar el workflow. No se necesita guardar un token personal: Actions usa sus credenciales automáticas con los permisos específicos de Pages. Open-Meteo no necesita una clave para este uso no comercial.

Pages está disponible en repositorios públicos gratuitos; la API tiene condiciones y límites de uso. El diseño requiere normalmente tres peticiones diarias y runners estándar. Las condiciones deben revisarse antes de ampliar el alcance: Pages, Actions y Open-Meteo.

Solución publicada: verificada con HTTP 200, descarga del CSV y consulta de metadata.json. Los metadatos del primer despliegue identificaron el commit 27263e7db878d735305ba78006d770919a249847, 90 filas y origen real Open-Meteo.

Ejecución exitosa de CI/CD: los jobs test, build y deploy terminaron correctamente. El workflow también comprueba por HTTP que el sitio sirve metadatos del commit que acaba de desplegarse.

Resultados comprobados

En la ejecución local del 1 de noviembre de 2026, el pipeline recuperó 90 registros reales para el período del 26 de septiembre al 25 de octubre de 2026: 30 por ciudad. Construyó los dos modelos y superó las nueve pruebas dbt. También pasaron cuatro pruebas unitarias y la comprobación de idempotencia con agregados sintéticos conocidos.

La ejecución remota también completó las pruebas y publicó el mismo período. La consulta directa del CSV público devolvió estos resultados:

Ciudad Días Promedio del punto medio diario (°C) Precipitación acumulada (mm)
Arequipa 30 17.48 1.1
Cusco 30 14.30 17.7
Lima 30 22.74 7.7

Son una instantánea del período 2026-09-26 a 2026-10-25, no valores permanentes. El reporte permite descargar el detalle y el resumen; sus metadatos indican el origen, las fechas, el momento de generación y el commit. Las pruebas locales y la comprobación HTTP del despliegue aportan evidencias separadas del funcionamiento.

Conclusión

El proyecto recorre el ciclo de un pipeline ELT: extracción, almacenamiento, transformación, validación, exportación y despliegue automatizado comprobado. Su tamaño permite explicar cada decisión y repetir el proceso sin administrar servidores.

La solución ya puede consultarse públicamente y actualizarse con cada ejecución exitosa del workflow. Como mejoras futuras quedan un histórico incremental, alertas ante fallos y pruebas sobre cambios de esquema en la API.

Datos de Open-Meteo, con atribución bajo CC BY 4.0.

Mi objetivo fue construir un flujo pequeño que convierta respuestas meteorológicas en dos productos: una tabla diaria limpia y un resumen por ciudad. El resultado se exporta a un reporte HTML y archivos CSV.

Arquitectura y herramientas 

Open-Meteo → Python → JSON crudo + DuckDB raw.weather
                              ↓
                       dbt stg_weather
                              ↓
                       dbt city_summary
                              ↓
                    pruebas de calidad
                              ↓
                   HTML + CSV + metadatos
                              ↓
                   GitHub Pages, tras CD
  • Python 3.12 extrae respuestas HTTP, valida los datos y exporta los resultados.
  • DuckDB almacena tablas analíticas en un archivo, sin administrar un servidor.
  • dbt Core y dbt-duckdb gestionan las transformaciones SQL, sus dependencias y las pruebas.
  • GitHub Actions ejecuta CI, la actualización diaria y el despliegue.
  • GitHub Pages es el destino configurado para alojar el reporte estático públicamente.

No se utilizan servicios ni credenciales de AWS. La arquitectura usa GitHub como plataforma SaaS y no necesita un proceso Python funcionando permanentemente. Para esta escala, dbt permite demostrar transformación y calidad sin desplegar un orquestador de larga duración.

Implementación

1. Extraer una ventana consistente

La fuente es la API histórica de Open-Meteo. Para cada ciudad se solicitan temperatura máxima, mínima y precipitación diaria. La ventana termina siete días antes de la fecha actual en Lima para dejar margen a la disponibilidad del histórico.

Antes de cargar, Python comprueba las 30 fechas esperadas, las longitudes de las listas, valores numéricos finitos, coherencia entre mínima y máxima y precipitación no negativa. Cada petición tiene un timeout y hasta tres intentos. Si falla, la ejecución termina con error: no reemplaza los datos reales por datos sintéticos.

2. Cargar sin duplicar

Después de validar las tres ciudades, una transacción reemplaza raw.weather en DuckDB. Es una reconstrucción completa de una ventana pequeña. Repetir una ejecución no debe multiplicar registros.

Se conservan también las respuestas JSON para inspeccionar la fuente. Este diseño no pretende guardar un histórico incremental ilimitado: prioriza que el proyecto pueda entenderse, ejecutarse y evaluarse con facilidad.

3. Transformar con dbt

select city, min(date) as start_date, max(date) as end_date,
       count(*) as days,
       round(avg((temperature_max + temperature_min) / 2), 2) as mean_midpoint_c,
       round(max(temperature_max), 2) as highest_c,
       round(min(temperature_min), 2) as lowest_c,
       round(sum(precipitation_mm), 2) as total_precipitation_mm
from {{ ref('stg_weather') }}
group by city

El indicador mean_midpoint_c es el promedio del punto medio entre mínima y máxima diaria. Lo etiqueté así porque no equivale a calcular una media de temperaturas horarias. La fuente contiene reanálisis; tampoco debe presentarse como medición de una estación local.

4. Probar y generar la salida

dbt build construye dos modelos y ejecuta nueve pruebas de datos: campos obligatorios, unicidad, duplicados, rangos y continuidad de la ventana. Solo después se exportan el reporte y los CSV.

Las pruebas unitarias de Python cubren respuestas válidas, mediciones inválidas, fechas incorrectas y fallos de red. El modo --offline usa una fixture sintética identificada como TEST y escribe en otra carpeta. CI lo ejecuta dos veces para comprobar idempotencia y agregados conocidos.

Para reproducirlo en Linux o macOS con Python 3.12:

python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python -m pipeline.run --offline --end-date 2026-01-30
python -m pipeline.run

El README incluye los comandos equivalentes para PowerShell. El reporte real queda en site/public/index.html.

Despliegue y automatización

El workflow versionado separa tres trabajos. test ejecuta pruebas y datos sintéticos. build depende de las pruebas y utiliza la API real. deploy publica exclusivamente site/public en Pages y comprueba el endpoint público por HTTP.

Las PR solo ejecutan pruebas. Un push a main, una ejecución manual o la programación diaria producen una nueva actualización real. La programación está configurada a las 06:17 de Lima; GitHub puede retrasar ejecuciones programadas.

Para activar la publicación hay que seleccionar Settings → Pages → Source → GitHub Actions en el repositorio y ejecutar el workflow. No se necesita guardar un token personal: Actions usa sus credenciales automáticas con los permisos específicos de Pages. Open-Meteo no necesita una clave para este uso no comercial.

Pages está disponible en repositorios públicos gratuitos; la API tiene condiciones y límites de uso. El diseño requiere normalmente tres peticiones diarias y runners estándar. Las condiciones deben revisarse antes de ampliar el alcance: Pages, Actions y Open-Meteo.

Solución publicada: verificada con HTTP 200, descarga del CSV y consulta de metadata.json. Los metadatos del primer despliegue identificaron el commit 27263e7db878d735305ba78006d770919a249847, 90 filas y origen real Open-Meteo.

Ejecución exitosa de CI/CD: los jobs test, build y deploy terminaron correctamente. El workflow también comprueba por HTTP que el sitio sirve metadatos del commit que acaba de desplegarse.

Resultados comprobados

En la ejecución local del 1 de noviembre de 2026, el pipeline recuperó 90 registros reales para el período del 26 de septiembre al 25 de octubre de 2026: 30 por ciudad. Construyó los dos modelos y superó las nueve pruebas dbt. También pasaron cuatro pruebas unitarias y la comprobación de idempotencia con agregados sintéticos conocidos.

La ejecución remota también completó las pruebas y publicó el mismo período. La consulta directa del CSV público devolvió estos resultados:

Ciudad Días Promedio del punto medio diario (°C) Precipitación acumulada (mm)
Arequipa 30 17.48 1.1
Cusco 30 14.30 17.7
Lima 30 22.74 7.7

Son una instantánea del período 2026-09-26 a 2026-10-25, no valores permanentes. El reporte permite descargar el detalle y el resumen; sus metadatos indican el origen, las fechas, el momento de generación y el commit. Las pruebas locales y la comprobación HTTP del despliegue aportan evidencias separadas del funcionamiento.

Conclusión

El proyecto recorre el ciclo de un pipeline ELT: extracción, almacenamiento, transformación, validación, exportación y despliegue automatizado comprobado. Su tamaño permite explicar cada decisión y repetir el proceso sin administrar servidores.

La solución ya puede consultarse públicamente y actualizarse con cada ejecución exitosa del workflow. Como mejoras futuras quedan un histórico incremental, alertas ante fallos y pruebas sobre cambios de esquema en la API.

title: # My Python Learning Journey – Understanding Python Fundamentals 🐍
summary:
Introduction

Today, I continued my Python learning journey and explored some important Python fundamentals.

As a beginner, I learned how objects, functions, methods, variables, and attributes work. I also explored function overloading, naming conventions, and PEP 8.

Let's look at what I learned today with simple examples.

1. What is an Object?

An object is an instance of a class.

In Python, almost everything is an object, including integers, strings, lists, and functions.

Example:

name = "Python"
age = 25

print(type(name))
print(type(age))

Here, "Python" is a string object and 25 is an integer object.

2. What is a Function?

A function is a reusable block of code that performs a particular task.

We use the def keyword to define a function.

Example:

def greet():
    print("Hello, Welcome to Python!")

greet()

Output:

Hello, Welcome to Python!

Here:

  • def is the keyword used to define a function.
  • greet is the function name.
  • greet() calls the function.

3. What is a Method?

A method is a function associated with an object or class.

Example:

name = "python"

print(name.upper())

Output:

PYTHON

Here, upper() is a string method that converts lowercase letters into uppercase letters.

4. What is a Variable?

A variable is a name that refers to an object.

Example:

name = "Sam"
age = 25

print(name)
print(age)

Here:

  • name refers to a string object.
  • age refers to an integer object.
  • = is the assignment operator.

5. What is an Attribute?

An attribute is a name associated with an object or class.

Attributes can store data or represent behavior.

Example:

class Student:

    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

s1 = Student("Sam", 25)

print(s1.name)
print(s1.age)

Here:

  • Student is a class.
  • s1 is an object (instance).
  • self refers to the current instance.
  • self.name and self.age are instance attributes.
  • __init__() is an initializer method.

6. What is an Instance?

An instance is an individual object created from a class.

Example:

class Student:
    pass

s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()

Here, s1 and s2 are two separate instances of the Student class.

A simple way to remember:

  • Class = Blueprint
  • Instance = Individual object created from that blueprint.

7. Class Attributes vs. Instance Attributes

Class Attribute

A class attribute is defined inside a class but outside its methods. It is shared by instances by default.

Instance Attribute

An instance attribute belongs to an individual object.

Example:

class Student:

    school = "ABC School"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

s1 = Student("Sam")
s2 = Student("David")

print(s1.school)
print(s2.school)

Output:

ABC School
ABC School

Both objects access the same class attribute.

Changing a class attribute through an object 

s1.school = "XYZ School"

print(s1.school)
print(s2.school)

Output:

XYZ School
ABC School

Here, Python creates an instance attribute named school for s1. It does not change the original class attribute.

Changing the class attribute 

Student.school = "DEF School"

print(s1.school)
print(s2.school)

Output:

XYZ School
DEF School

The s1 object continues using its own instance attribute, while s2 accesses the updated class attribute.

8. What is Function Overloading in Python?

Function overloading means using the same function name with different parameters.

Python does not support traditional function overloading directly. If we define multiple functions with the same name, the latest definition replaces the previous one.

We can achieve similar behavior using default arguments and *args.

Using default arguments 

def add(a, b, c=0):
    print(a + b + c)

add(10, 20)
add(10, 20, 30)

Output:

30
60

Using *args 

def add(*args):
    print(sum(args))

add(10, 20)
add(10, 20, 30)

Output:

30
60

*args allows a function to accept multiple positional arguments.

9. Naming Conventions in Python

Naming conventions are guidelines used to name variables, functions, classes, and constants.

Snake Case

Words are separated by underscores.

student_name = "Sam"

def calculate_total():
    pass

Commonly used for variables and functions.

Pascal Case

Each word starts with a capital letter.

class StudentDetails:
    pass

Commonly used for class names.

Camel Case

The first word starts with a lowercase letter, and subsequent words start with uppercase letters.

studentName = "Sam"

It is valid Python, but snake_case is preferred for variables and functions.

Upper Snake Case

All letters are uppercase, separated by underscores.

MAX_SIZE = 100
DATABASE_NAME = "StudentDB"

Commonly used for constants.

Leading Underscore

A single underscore at the beginning indicates that a name is intended for internal use.

_internal_value = 100

This is a convention, not strict access control.

10. What is PEP 8?

PEP stands for Python Enhancement Proposal.

PEP 8 is the Python style guide that provides recommendations for writing clean, readable, and consistent Python code.

Some important guidelines:

  1. Use four spaces for indentation.
  2. Use snake_case for variables and functions.
  3. Use PascalCase for class names.
  4. Use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants.
  5. Use spaces around operators.
  6. Separate functions and classes using blank lines.
  7. Keep code lines within the recommended length.

Example

Without following PEP 8:

def calculateTotal(a,b):
    total=a+b
    print(total)

Following PEP 8:

def calculate_total(a, b):
    total = a + b
    print(total)

The second example is easier to read and follows common Python style recommendations.

Conclusion

Today, I explored several important Python concepts, including objects, functions, methods, variables, attributes, instances, and class attributes.

I also learned about function overloading, naming conventions, and PEP 8.

Understanding these fundamentals is helping me build a strong foundation in Python.

I'm continuing my learning journey step by step and sharing my progress with the developer community.

title: How I Built a Lightweight Cloud IDE with a 1-Line Local PC Bridge and Live Preview on a $0 Budget
summary:
Every web developer knows this routine:

You want to test a quick HTML/CSS layout, inspect an SVG icon in a GitHub repository, or tweak a configuration file on a remote machine.

Your options?

  • Wait 15 seconds for a heavy desktop Electron IDE to boot up.
  • Spin up a heavy cloud container that takes 2 minutes and burns compute credits.
  • Open 4 terminal tabs to juggle git pull, git status, git commit, and local development servers.

I got tired of the friction, so over the past few weeks I built Hashtag Studio — a lightweight, zero-install browser IDE that bridges both GitHub repositories and your raw local PC drives side-by-side with instant live previews.

Here is the complete behind-the-scenes breakdown of how it's built, the architecture decisions, and the hardware battle scars along the way.

1. What Hashtag Studio Does

Hashtag Studio runs directly inside any modern browser with three core pillars:

  1. Instant GitHub Workspace: Connect via GitHub OAuth, instantly explore your repository files, view code with syntax highlighting, and commit changes back to GitHub in a single click (no terminal commands).
  2. Native PC Bridge (Zero-Install): For times when your code is on your local hard drive, you run a single 1-line PowerShell bridge command. Your browser instantly mounts your local drives (C:\, Documents, etc.) so you can browse, edit, and save files directly to local disk from the browser window.
  3. Responsive Device Simulators: Integrated live HTML/JS preview with 1-click switches between Desktop, Tablet, and Mobile viewport frames.
  4. Built-in AI Co-Pilot: Context-aware assistant to generate UI components, fix syntax errors, and refactor code directly inside your project.

2. The Architecture ($0 Cloud Bill)

Rather than paying $50/month for AWS EC2 or managed Kubernetes clusters, the entire backend runs on a dedicated, low-power headless Linux tower:

  • Zero-Port Tunneling: Instead of setting up port forwarding or exposing an IP address, traffic routes through an encrypted Cloudflare Tunnel. The server connects outbound to Cloudflare edge nodes, making the home IP completely invisible.
  • Lightweight Python Runtime: The backend is written in modular Python using native async I/O. Memory footprint stays under 120MB RAM, allowing it to respond in milliseconds.
  • Stateless Token Auth: Secure OAuth2 flow supporting both Google and GitHub with encrypted session cookies and persistent SQLite storage.

3. How the 1-Line Local PC Bridge Works

The hardest design challenge was: How do you let a web browser read and write files on a user's Windows PC without forcing them to install a 300MB Electron desktop app?

When a user clicks "Connect Local PC", the server generates a cryptographically signed, short-lived session token and outputs a clean 1-line command:

irm "https://core.hashtagai.online/connect.ps1?token=..." | iex

Under the hood:

  1. The script establishes an authenticated session over HTTPS back to the Studio server.
  2. It exposes lightweight disk endpoints bounded strictly to the user's active session.
  3. The browser Studio UI immediately populates with local drive letters (C:\, D:) and standard directories (Desktop, Documents).
  4. Edits in the browser trigger atomic writes directly onto the physical local disk.

4. Engineering Battle Scars

Building on a low-power home server produced some wild low-level bugs that took days to track down:

  1. The Ghost Wi-Fi Disconnects: The server's USB Wi-Fi adapter kept dropping off the local network every 30 minutes with AP deauth reason=4. It turned out the Linux kernel was automatically putting the Realtek USB dongle into low-power autosuspend after 2 seconds of network idle. Adding usbcore.autosuspend=-1 and a non-destructive 3-second ping pulse keepalive permanently cured the connection drops.
  2. Broken Pipe Resilience: Fast client navigation triggered unhandled BrokenPipeError exceptions when streaming assets. We wrapped socket writes with graceful connection-reset handlers to prevent thread starvation.

5. Try It Live (Free Demo)

Hashtag Studio is live, free, and runs right now in your browser:

🔗 Live Studio: core.hashtagai.online/studio

There is a 💬 Feedback button in the bottom statusbar. If you take it for a spin, I’d love to know:

  • How fast does the live preview load your HTML/JS?
  • Would you use the 1-line PowerShell bridge for editing local files?
  • What features would you like to see next?

Drop your thoughts in the comments below!

title: Why My ESF-551 Scale Kept Disconnecting from Home Assistant: Japan's Measurement Act
summary:
I connected an Etekcity ESF-551, a BLE body scale, to Home Assistant, and not a single measurement arrived. I had Claude Code chase the cause, and it ended at Article 9 of Japan's Measurement Act. Units sold in Japan have the unit switch removed because of that law.

I know nothing about firmware or law. What I did was step on the scale and decide what to have it look into next. Without AI, I couldn't have done this investigation.

Nothing comes back when I step on it

I used the HACS integration etekcity_fitness_scale_ble, which wraps etekcity_esf551_ble==0.8.4. Claude Code read the log: it showed the integration connecting, reading the HW/SW versions, writing the unit command a5220305002b0163a10000 (unit 0, kg), and getting disconnected about 0.4 seconds later. Then it reconnected and did it again. No notification ever came when I stepped on the scale, and every sensor stayed unavailable.

It happened even when the command changed nothing, kg to kg.

Skip one command and it works

I left the narrowing down to it too. Claude Code subscribed to 0000fff1 from another machine with plain bleak and left out only the unit write. No disconnect. While I stood on the scale, 22-byte notifications arrived about every 45 ms, around 80 of them.

So Claude Code wrote a local patch that passes display_unit=None and skips the write. All 14 sensors filled in. I had it write the upstream issue too, and filed it (etekcity_esf551_ble #15).

Up to here it was a story about fixing a library bug.

Only the US manual has a unit setting

I had it look for why only the Japanese version lacks a unit switch. The VeSync app has no unit setting, while the US manual has the steps.

Putting the back label next to the US spec showed this was a different market variant, not just a firmware revision. Japanese devices and IoT, again, I thought.

US ESF-551 The unit I bought in Japan
Capacity 400 lb / 180 kg 2–150 kg
Resolution 0.05 lb / 0.02 kg 100 g
Radio approval FCC ID 2AB22-ESF551 Giteki R 210-252428
Measurement Act none household "正" mark

Claude Code also pulled the Measurement Act from the e-Gov law API and read it. Article 9 forbids selling, or displaying for sale, a measuring instrument marked in non-statutory units. A scale that can show lb or st can't be sold in Japan, so manufacturers drop the unit-switch feature from the Japanese firmware. Weighing myself is neither a transaction nor a certification, so Article 8 doesn't touch the user. Only the seller is bound.

The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry's FY2015 test-purchase report even has a real case: a vendor who didn't know pounds and stones were prohibited was told to seal the device so it couldn't be switched.

Whether the disconnect is deliberate, I don't know

What I know is why the Japanese version has no unit switch. I can't tell whether the disconnect itself is intended, or just firmware that doesn't know the command and drops the link sloppily. Removing the feature is fine. I just suspect it was removed carelessly. I only have one unit, so I can't say that model identifier 12 in the manufacturer data marks the Japanese variant. For upstream I suggested registering identifier 12 with display_unit_settable=False so the write is skipped, and left the call to the maintainer.

An experiment that sends an unknown opcode to see how it disconnects is still undone.

Fixed the next day

The day after I filed the issue, the maintainer replied.

That's interesting to know about that Japanese regulation. That would explain it I guess, and since the option doesn't even show up in the app that pretty much confirms it I think.

Library v0.8.8 and the HA integration 0.8.3 came out the same day. I updated the integration to 0.8.3, removed my local patch, stepped on the scale, and the measurements came through. That was surprisingly fast, and I'm grateful.

Self-hosting Home Assistant is a chore. But it brings lessons like this one, from a bathroom scale all the way to a statute, and I'm glad I do it.

This post was written with AI assistance and reviewed by the author.
